ONE OF THE TWO MAVAL SEAPLANES WHICH FAILED IN FLIGHT.

S/111Al00 -On Monday, August 31st, two naval giant sea-
planes, the P.N.9 No.1 and the P.N.9 No.3
took off from San Fransisco buy on an attempted
non-stop flight to Hawaii. The course was car-
fully napped out by the Navy Department, and
was guarded by warships stationed at 200 mile
intervals all the way to Pearl Harbor, Hawaii.
Both naval planes made good time and progress
during the first few hundred miles out; but
on the afternoon of the second day, the P.N.9
No. 1 was reported missing; while the P.N.9 No.
3 had been forced to abandon the flight for
lack of fuel.

Photo shows the P.N.9 No.3 commanded by Licoutenant Alan
Snody, which was forced to give up its non-
stop Hawaiian flight in the early stages.

PLANE THAT WILL ATTEMPT NON-STOP FLIGHT FROM PACIFIC
COAT TO HONOLULU.

S/100X526 -The Boeing PB-1 seaplane, built at Seattle, for the non-stop flight from the American mainland to Honolulu scheduled for next Monday. This new seaplane incorporates radical departures in airplane construction and when the giant Boeing plane lifted its 12 tons of steel and wood from the waters of Seattle Bay it represented a new milestone in American Airplane production. The Boeing plant, which built the craft, is one of the three leading manufacturers of planes in the U.S. znd has been the largest constructor of government planes.

WATCH YOUR CREDIT LINE. (SLUG) HAMILIAN FLIGHT. PHOTO BY UNDERWOOD & UNDERWOOD, NEW YORK.

Two giant naval planes, the P.N.9 No. 1, and the P.N.9 No.3, set out from San Fransisco on the afternoon of Monday, August 31, in an effort to make a non-stop flight to Hawaii, a distance of 2100 nautical miles. The flight was under the careful direction of the Navy Department, with ADMiral Moffett in San Fransisco to personally supervise matters, and with a series of destroyers stationed at 200 mile intervals all the way to Hawaii. Commander John Rodgers was first pilot of the P.N.9 No.1 and commander of the venture; while Lieutenant Alan Snody commanded the P.N.9No.3. In addition to the two P.N.9 phanes a large Boeing plane, the P.B.l, was prevented from making the start on Monday due to need for repairs. The P.B.l is still in readiness at San Fransisco to follow the first two planes; but is being held back until the outcome of the leaders is seen. During the first few hundred miles from San Fransisco, the two daring planes sailed smoothly westward with all conditions auguring well for their enterprise. But on the afternoon of Septemberl, the second day out, Commander Wilbur R. Van Auken of the U.S.S.Arocstock, one of the warships assigned to the course, reported that he had lost touch with the P.N.9 No.1. Immediately all available methods were used to locate the missing plane; but up the present time no word whatsoever has been received as to its fate. Meanwhile the other plane, the P.N.9 No.3 was forced down for lack of fuel.

PHOTO OF--THE NO-4 OFF FOR THE AZORES AND THE HARBOR AT TREPASSEY FROM WHICH IT MADE THE START.

These are the first official photographs to be received here from Trepassey Bay, Newfoundland showing the start of the U.S. Naval fliers on their epoch-making journey across the Atlantic Ocean. The American Naval seaplane NO-4, under the command of Lisutenant Commander Albert C. Read, is here shown skimming thru the water of Trepassey Bay, Newfoundland at the start of the flight to the Azores. Washington officially credits the plans with having mads the 1,200 miles flight in 15 hours and 13 minutes. The lower photo shows the aviation camp and the Bay at Trepassey as seen from a Naval seaplane.

MAIL PLANE CAUGHT BY AIR CURRENT
PLUNGES INTO ROCKY MOUNTAINS,

Taking off from Rock Springs field and headed for Salt Lake City, Utah, with the regular westbound mail, this government eviator in his plane was caught in a terrific down draft while 9,200 feet in the air and 2,000 feet above the Rocky Mountains, and plunged downward at a great speed into the side of the mountain slope. After striking the ground the plane slid backward about fifty feet and stopped at an angle of eighty degrees, the side of the mountain being almost perpendicular. Three mechanics who rushed the plane were forced to climb to the top of the mountain and there formed a human chain to rescue the lone pilot, R.H. Ellis, who was stranded for many hours. Photo shows the plane as it was left in the snow.

PHOTO OF THE REMAINS OF AMERICA'S FINEST AIRSHIP.

-The giant naval a irship Shenandoah which left Lake-hurst,N.J, Wednesday afternoon for St.Louis, was caught in a storm while cruising above the small town of Pleasant City, Ohio, and broke into three pieces by the gale, which equalled in intensity a small hurricane. The first effect of the crash was to loosen the control cabin which was linked to the forward section of the ship, and in which were most of the officers, including Commander Lansdowne. The loosened gondola fell to the ground with a crash killing every one of the thirteen men it contained. The remainder of this same forward section drifted away from the main body of the ship like a fee balloon, and finally landed safely twclvc miles away. Meanwhile, the body of the ship fell immediately after the break, but caused the death of only one man. In all 14 officers and men were killed and two were injured. This photo shows the different parts of the wreck taken immediately after the accident, with the crowd assembled around the main body of the Shenandoah which fell straight down after the crash. Note the well preserved and distinctly readable name and naval insignia of the ill-fated craft.
